documents.title: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Management of Chronic Pancreatitis

chunks.content: Introduction and background Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a progressive fibro-inflammatory disease characterized by irreversible structural damage to the pancreas, leading to exocrine and endocrine dysfunction in individuals with genetic susceptibility or environmental risk factors [ , ]. Abdominal pain is the most common and clinically relevant manifestation of CP and represents a major contributor to healthcare utilization and impaired quality of life (QoL). Pain in CP results from pancreatic inflammation, fibrosis, ductal hypertension, and perineural changes that activate and sensitize nociceptors, with progression to central sensitization and altered pain processing. Consequently, pain may become chronic and partially independent of structural pancreatic damage. Despite advances in understanding disease mechanisms and the availability of multiple therapeutic options, pain in CP remains challenging to manage, with considerable variability in clinical practice and outcomes. This review aims to provide a comprehensive, clinically oriented overview of pain in CP by summarizing current concepts of pain pathophysiology and critically assessing available medical, endoscopic, and surgical management strategies. In particular, it seeks to address gaps in the existing literature by integrating emerging insights into pain mechanisms with pragmatic treatment algorithms, highlighting areas where evidence is limited or conflicting, and clarifying how available data complement, rather than duplicate, existing guidelines and prior reviews. Epidemiology Pain is reported in approximately 60-80% of patients during CP. Longitudinal data indicate that ~85% of patients develop persistent pain within four to five years of disease onset, while up to 60% continue to experience painful episodes beyond 10 years [ - ]. The prevalence of pain is particularly high in Asian populations, with Indian cohorts reporting rates exceeding 90%. The etiological distribution of CP varies by geographic region. Alcohol remains the predominant cause in Western countries, whereas idiopathic chronic pancreatitis (ICP) is the most common etiology in India, although alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis (ACP) is increasingly recognized [ , ]. Pain is more frequently reported as a presenting symptom in ICP than in alcoholic CP. Over 90% of patients with both early- and late-onset ICP present with pain; however, pain onset occurs earlier in early-onset disease, whereas late-onset ICP is associated with higher rates of diabetes mellitus and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency [ ]. Pain in CP is heterogeneous, manifesting as intermittent or persistent symptoms reflecting underlying pathophysiological differences [ ]. European cohorts predominantly describe intermittent pain patterns, while persistent pain correlates with structural complications, increased healthcare utilization, disability, and impaired QoL, with active smoking being a consistent adverse prognostic factor [ , ]. Pain burnout is more likely in late-onset, non-calcific, idiopathic disease with intermittent pain and absence of ductal obstruction, particularly among non-smokers, and often parallels progression to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency or diabetes mellitus, reflecting glandular burnout [ , ]. Review Search methodology A comprehensive narrative literature search was conducted to identify key evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and management of pain in CP. Major electronic databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, were searched from database inception to December 2025, using relevant Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms such as CP, pain, analgesic therapy, endoscopic interventions, celiac plexus block, and surgical management. Reference lists of pertinent review articles, consensus statements, and international clinical practice guidelines were manually screened to identify additional relevant publications. Studies were selected for inclusion based on clinical relevance and contribution to understanding pain mechanisms or informing management strategies, with an emphasis on randomized controlled trials, high-quality observational studies, systematic reviews, and guideline documents published in English. Given the narrative (non-systematic) nature of this review, formal inclusion-exclusion criteria and quantitative quality assessment of individual studies were not applied, and the search strategy is inherently subject to selection bias. Pathophysiology of pain Pain in CP is multifactorial, arising from pancreatic or extrapancreatic sources, including nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms that often overlap. This complexity frequently contributes to treatment failure (Figure ) [ , ]. Nociceptive pain results from pancreatic tissue injury and inflammation, whereas neuropathic pain arises from damage to pancreatic or extrapancreatic nerves. Nociceptive pain in CP results from activation of nociceptors by tissue injury and inflammation, with peripheral sensitization lowering pain thresholds. This process is sustained by neurogenic inflammation, cytokines, proteases, and mediators that act on ion channels, such as transient receptor potential vanilloid (TRPV) 1 and 4, and voltage-gated A-type (IA) potassium currents (Figure ). Other substances, like transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1), platelet-derived growth factor B (PDGF-B), and glycoprotein 130 (GP130), are present; patients complain of dull, sharp, or nagging pain in the upper abdomen with radiation to the back [ , ]. Neuropathic pain in CP results from injury-induced modifications in pancreatic and peripancreatic nerve signaling. It is driven by neuroplasticity, neural remodeling, neuritis, inflammatory infiltration, and dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-mediated amplification of pain, with C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12/C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCL12/CXCR4) signaling further enhancing neuro-immune sensitization (Figure ). The

Other substances, like transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1), platelet-derived growth factor B (PDGF-B), and glycoprotein 130 (GP130), are present; patients complain of dull, sharp, or nagging pain in the upper abdomen with radiation to the back [ , ]. Neuropathic pain in CP results from injury-induced modifications in pancreatic and peripancreatic nerve signaling. It is driven by neuroplasticity, neural remodeling, neuritis, inflammatory infiltration, and dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-mediated amplification of pain, with C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12/C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCL12/CXCR4) signaling further enhancing neuro-immune sensitization (Figure ). The DRG amplifies pancreatic pain through maladaptive neuroplasticity and sustained nociceptive signaling. Upregulated CXCL12/CXCR4 enhances neuro-immune sensitization, making DRG pathways promising therapeutic targets [ , ]. Over time, pain may become independent of ongoing pancreatic injury, resembling a neuropathic pain state influenced by psychological and psychosocial factors, which explains the poor correlation between structural disease severity and pain intensity. Altered descending inhibitory pathways and enhanced facilitatory pathways further perpetuate chronic pain. Cross-organ sensitization may also account for overlapping functional gastrointestinal symptoms seen in many patients. Nociplastic pain in CP arises from altered central pain processing rather than ongoing tissue injury or nerve damage. It is driven by central sensitization, impaired descending inhibitory pathways, and persistent amplification of pain signals within the spinal cord and brain. Central sensitization develops through sustained nociceptive input, leading to amplified pain processing and persistence of pain independent of ongoing tissue injury. This mechanism also explains the disproportionate severity of pain relative to structural pancreatic disease (Figure ) [ , ]. Neuroplastic changes, including neural hypertrophy, altered neurotransmission, and viscerosomatic convergence, also contribute to persistent and widespread pain. There are two distinct types of clinical manifestations of pain in CP. The "A-type pain," or intermittent pain, is characterized by discrete episodes of pain with pain-free periods in between. The "B-type pain" is described as persistent background pain with episodes of acute exacerbation. Studies have shown that intermittent pain responds more predictably to treatment than the latter type ("B-type pain") [ , ]. Hence, the pathophysiology of pain in CP reflects a dynamic interplay between peripheral pancreatic injury and progressive central nervous system reorganization. While early pain is driven by inflammation, fibrosis, ductal hypertension, and perineural changes that sensitize pancreatic nociceptors, persistent nociceptive input ultimately promotes central sensitization, impaired descending inhibitory control, and maladaptive brain pain processing. As a result, pain may assume a chronic, neuropathic-like phenotype that is increasingly dissociated from structural pancreatic abnormalities. This mechanistic evolution accounts for the poor correlation between imaging findings and pain severity and highlights the necessity for individualized, mechanism-based, multimodal therapeutic approaches [ , ]. Management Goals of Treatment The primary goals of therapy for pain in CP are to achieve durable pain relief, improve QoL, and restore functional capacity while minimizing treatment-related morbidity. Management is best conceptualized as a combination of non-interventional and interventional strategies guided by the dominant pain mechanism [ , ]. Non-interventional therapy focuses on attenuating pancreatic stimulation and inflammation through lifestyle modification, PERT, and analgesic and neuromodulatory agents to address inflammatory, neuropathic, and centrally sensitized pain. Interventional treatments target pancreatic ductal hypertension and local complications, with endoscopic or surgical ductal decompression reserved for patients with obstructive large-duct disease or refractory pain. Across both approaches, preservation of residual pancreatic exocrine and endocrine function, prevention of disease progression, and reduction of long-term opioid dependence remain central objectives, supported by a stepwise, mechanism-based treatment paradigm [ ]. Accordingly, the goal of pain management in CP should extend beyond reduction in pain scores to include improved QoL, minimization of opioid dependence, and the sustained ability to engage in daily activities. Non-interventional Therapy Non-interventional therapy should be tried in all patients with CP-related pain because pain mechanisms are multifactorial and often include inflammatory, neuropathic, and centrally mediated components that may respond to medical management. Early conservative treatment can reduce symptoms, limit opioid use, and help identify patients unlikely to benefit from invasive ductal or surgical interventions. Non-pharmacologic Measures Core non-pharmacologic measures include strict alcohol abstinence and smoking cessation, consistently recommended because both exposures worsen the disease course and are associated with pain exacerbations. Structured nutrition support (small, frequent meals; individualized fat restriction when symptomatic; correction of vitamin and micronutrient deficiencies) and treatment of comorbid anxiety/depression and sleep disturbance are also important for reducing the pain burden and improving function (Table ) [ , ]. Alcohol exacerbates pain in CP by perpetuating pancreatic inflammation, increasing ductal obstruction and intraductal pressure, and promoting neural hypertrophy and central sensitization. Active smoking independently accelerates fibrosis and perineural inflammation, worsens neuropathic pain, and reduces responsiveness to medical, endoscopic, and surgical therapies, making abstinence from both exposures essential for pain control. Current society guidance emphasizes a multidisciplinary approach that integrates lifestyle modification, nutrition, and stepwise analgesia before

Alcohol exacerbates pain in CP by perpetuating pancreatic inflammation, increasing ductal obstruction and intraductal pressure, and promoting neural hypertrophy and central sensitization. Active smoking independently accelerates fibrosis and perineural inflammation, worsens neuropathic pain, and reduces responsiveness to medical, endoscopic, and surgical therapies, making abstinence from both exposures essential for pain control. Current society guidance emphasizes a multidisciplinary approach that integrates lifestyle modification, nutrition, and stepwise analgesia before escalating to invasive therapies [ , ]. Pharmacologic Measures Pharmacologic conservative therapy generally follows a step-up strategy (often aligned pragmatically with the WHO analgesic ladder), prioritizing acetaminophen (when appropriate) and adjuvant agents over long-term opioids. Analgesic therapy should use oral, around-the-clock dosing guided by pain severity and drug pharmacokinetics, with individualized dose adjustment and strict adherence to balance efficacy and side effects and prevent pain recurrence [ ]. Because a large component of CP pain is neuropathic/centrally mediated, neuromodulators (gabapentin/pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are commonly used; notably, pregabalin demonstrated superiority to placebo for pain reduction in a randomized controlled trial and remains a key evidence-based option for selected patients [ ]. If opioids are required, many experts recommend using the lowest effective dose, reassessing frequently, and integrating non-opioid adjuvants to minimize opioid exposure. Most patients with CP do not achieve adequate pain control with non-opioid analgesics, leading to high reliance on advanced therapies; approximately three-quarters require opioid medications, nearly two-thirds undergo endoscopic interventions, and about one-third ultimately require surgical management. Optimal pain control requires a mechanism-based approach: nociceptive pain is best addressed with stepwise analgesia, lifestyle modification, and pancreatic ductal decompression via endoscopic or surgical methods; neuropathic pain responds more favorably to neuromodulators such as gabapentinoids and targeted interventions like celiac plexus blockade; while nociplastic pain benefits from multimodal strategies including structured physical activity, cognitive-behavioral therapy, mind-body interventions, antidepressants (e.g., duloxetine or tricyclics), acupuncture, and emerging neuromodulation techniques [ ]. Adjunctive Therapies Adjunctive therapies may be considered on a case-by-case basis. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) is the standard treatment for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) in CP and provides symptomatic relief by improving digestion and nutrient absorption. While it effectively reduces steatorrhea, diarrhea, and meal-related discomfort, its role in direct pain control is limited and inconsistent. PERT does not modify underlying inflammation or fibrosis and is therefore used as an adjunct to comprehensive pain management and lifestyle interventions to improve QoL [ ]. Evidence does not support routine PERT solely for pain relief (particularly with enteric-coated preparations), so its role in analgesia is limited to selected scenarios and comorbidity management. Antioxidants have shown mixed results across trials and meta-analyses (including Cochrane data) and are best considered an optional adjunct in carefully selected patients rather than routine care [ ]. Throughout conservative management, clinicians should reassess the pain phenotype, nutritional status, and psychosocial contributors, and refer for endoscopic or surgical evaluation only when a clear anatomic driver (e.g., obstructed main pancreatic duct (MPD)) is identified or when conservative measures fail. In large-duct CP, pain is predominantly driven by ductal obstruction and intraductal hypertension; conservative therapy provides supportive relief but often serves as a bridge to endoscopic or surgical ductal decompression. In small-duct CP, pain is largely nociplastic or neuropathic in origin; conservative management with enzymes, neuromodulators, antioxidants, and psychosocial interventions remains the cornerstone of long-term pain control [ , ]. Interventional management ERCP-Guided Management Pain due to ductal obstruction with hypertension is the predominant nociceptive mechanism in patients with the large-duct phenotype, thus requiring ductal decompression (Table ). Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)-guided ductal decompression is recommended as the first-line therapy for obstructive CP with ductal dilation due to stones or strictures, with optimal outcomes achieved through complete and sustained ductal decompression, particularly in large-duct disease (MPD ≥5-6 mm) (Figure ). Conversely, ERCP is ineffective and not recommended in small-duct or non-obstructive disease, where pain is more likely to be neuropathic or centrally mediated. Across multiple studies, ERCP achieves technical success rates of approximately 70-90%, while clinical success, defined as meaningful pain relief, varies according to the underlying ductal pathology. Pain improvement is reported in 65-80% of patients with isolated ductal stones, 60-75% of those with dominant strictures, and decreases to <50-60% in patients with multiple strictures or combined complex disease. Importantly, durable pain relief correlates strongly with complete ductal clearance and sustained ductal decompression, rather than partial or transient interventions. In patients with large or impacted pancreatic duct stones (>5 mm), especially in the head or body, extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) facilitates stone fragmentation and subsequent endoscopic extraction. Staged ERCP within 24-72 hours is preferred for optimal clearance. Pancreatoscopy-directed intracorporeal lithotripsy is reserved for radiolucent,

underlying ductal pathology. Pain improvement is reported in 65-80% of patients with isolated ductal stones, 60-75% of those with dominant strictures, and decreases to <50-60% in patients with multiple strictures or combined complex disease. Importantly, durable pain relief correlates strongly with complete ductal clearance and sustained ductal decompression, rather than partial or transient interventions. In patients with large or impacted pancreatic duct stones (>5 mm), especially in the head or body, extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) facilitates stone fragmentation and subsequent endoscopic extraction. Staged ERCP within 24-72 hours is preferred for optimal clearance. Pancreatoscopy-directed intracorporeal lithotripsy is reserved for radiolucent, impacted, or ESWL-refractory stones, preferably using laser lithotripsy, and should be considered a salvage option in expert centers [ , , ]. ERCP is most effective for single, dominant strictures in the pancreatic head or proximal body with upstream ductal dilation. Long-segment, multiple strictures or those associated with an inflammatory head mass respond poorly to endotherapy, and repeated ERCP in these settings often delays definitive management without durable pain relief [ ]. ERCP-based therapy should be discontinued when pain persists despite adequate ductal decompression, when stones or strictures recur rapidly despite optimized therapy, or when endoscopic treatment extends beyond 6-12 months without sustained clinical benefit. Temporary pancreatic duct stenting may provide short-term symptom relief or serve as a bridge to ESWL or surgery in patients with incomplete stone clearance; however, long-term stenting without definitive ductal clearance is not disease-modifying and should not be pursued as a stand-alone strategy. Several factors have been identified as predictors of futility of ERCP for pain control, including small-duct disease, multiple or diffuse strictures, extensive parenchymal fibrosis, long disease duration, opioid dependence, and features of central sensitization. Early recognition of these predictors is critical to avoid repeated ineffective endoscopic interventions and to facilitate timely referral for alternative therapeutic strategies [ ]. Collectively, current evidence supports a step-up, mechanism-based approach to pain management in CP, in which ERCP remains the first-line interventional therapy for obstructive disease, supplemented by ESWL and advanced endoscopic techniques when indicated, withEndoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided interventions and surgery reserved for carefully selected patients who fail conventional endotherapy. EUS-Guided Interventions EUS-guided therapeutic interventions play an essential role in the management of pain in CP, particularly in patients with persistent symptoms despite optimized medical therapy and who are not immediate candidates for surgery (Figure ). These are classified as neural (celiac plexus block or neurolysis) or pancreas-directed approaches, including EUS-guided pancreatic duct drainage (EUS-PPD) and rendezvous techniques [ , ]. Neural (Analgesic) EUS-Guided Interventions Neural interventions include EUS-guided celiac plexus block (EUS-CPB) and EUS-guided celiac plexus neurolysis (EUS-CPN). EUS-CPB involves the injection of a local anesthetic with or without a corticosteroid around the celiac plexus or ganglia under real-time ultrasound guidance. It is indicated for patients with refractory pain despite ductal decompression or surgery, those without significant ductal obstruction, or early disease dominated by inflammatory neural sensitization (Figure ) [ , , ]. Performed under sedation, EUS-CPB uses anatomical landmarks including the aorta, celiac axis, and superior mesenteric artery, with injection of bupivacaine followed by triamcinolone using central or bilateral techniques. The procedure is generally safe, with mostly mild, transient adverse effects, and provides superior short-term pain relief compared with CT-guided approaches, although benefits are typically temporary. Clinical response is variable and usually lasts weeks to months, supporting EUS-CPB as a palliative or adjunctive therapy rather than a definitive treatment. Better outcomes are seen in patients with visceral pain, shorter disease duration, and lower opioid requirements, while those with central sensitization respond poorly. Repeated blocks may be considered in responders, but failure after one or two sessions should prompt consideration of definitive surgical management. Pancreas-Directed EUS-Guided Interventions Advanced EUS-guided pancreatic duct procedures, like EUS-guided rendezvous techniques and direct EUS-PDD, are options for certain patients with blocked ducts who have not had success with ERCP (Figure ). These procedures help relieve pressure in direct transmural drainage (pancreaticogastrostomy or pancreaticoduodenostomy), which is technically demanding and should be limited to high-volume expert centers. EUS-guided rendezvous drainage involves EUS puncture of the pancreatic duct with guidewire passage across the papilla to enable transpapillary ERCP drainage, restoring physiological flow while preserving ductal anatomy and avoiding permanent transmural fistulae [ ]. EUS-PDD entails duct puncture, pancreatography, tract dilation, and transmural stenting; most experts recommend an MPD ≥5 mm for safety and efficacy. Plastic stents (5-7 Fr) are standard, with fully covered self-expandable metal stents (FCSEMS) or lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS) reserved for refractory cases in expert centers. Technical success rates range from 82% to 95%, with clinical pain improvement in 80% to 93% of successful cases, particularly in patients with dilated ducts, clear obstruction, and limited central sensitization. Adverse events occur in 15-20% (pancreatitis, leak, infection, bleeding, perforation), reinforcing the need for careful selection and expert performance. These techniques are best

EUS-PDD entails duct puncture, pancreatography, tract dilation, and transmural stenting; most experts recommend an MPD ≥5 mm for safety and efficacy. Plastic stents (5-7 Fr) are standard, with fully covered self-expandable metal stents (FCSEMS) or lumen-apposing metal stents (LAMS) reserved for refractory cases in expert centers. Technical success rates range from 82% to 95%, with clinical pain improvement in 80% to 93% of successful cases, particularly in patients with dilated ducts, clear obstruction, and limited central sensitization. Adverse events occur in 15-20% (pancreatitis, leak, infection, bleeding, perforation), reinforcing the need for careful selection and expert performance. These techniques are best considered salvage, anatomy-preserving options within a stepwise, mechanism-based approach, with surgery reserved for recurrent stent dysfunction or persistent symptoms [ , ]. Complication-Directed EUS-Guided Interventions EUS-guided drainage of pancreatic pseudocysts and walled-off collections has been shown to significantly reduce pain when symptoms are driven by mass effect, ductal obstruction, or ongoing inflammation, particularly in patients who are poor surgical candidates. Significantly, the effectiveness of EUS-guided therapeutic interventions for pain in CP depends heavily on proper patient selection and a clear understanding of the underlying pain mechanisms, as outcomes are superior when nociceptive drivers are addressed rather than when pain is predominantly neuropathic or centrally mediated. Consequently, EUS-guided therapies should be viewed as integral components of a multidisciplinary, mechanism-based approach to refractory pain management in CP rather than as stand-alone treatments [ , ]. Surgery Surgical management of CP includes decompression, resection, or combined procedures, selected according to pancreatic pathology. Although optimal timing remains debated, surgery should ideally be performed within two to three years of disease onset and before central sensitization develops. A step-up approach is recommended for large-duct disease, whereas small-duct disease warrants early surgical consideration with neuromodulatory strategies (Figure ). Large-Duct Disease Surgery is indicated for persistent pain refractory to medical and endoscopic therapy, a markedly dilated MPD (≥7 mm), an inflammatory head mass, complications (biliary/duodenal obstruction), or suspected malignancy. Longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (Partington-Rochelle) is preferred for uniformly dilated ducts without a head mass. Head-dominant disease is best managed with combined drainage-resection procedures (Frey or Beger), which provide effective pain control with lower morbidity and better preservation of pancreatic function than pancreaticoduodenectomy. Pancreaticoduodenectomy is reserved for suspected malignancy or extensive head disease. Early surgery offers superior and more durable pain relief and quality-of-life benefits compared with endotherapy [ - ]. Small-Duct Disease In patients with MPD <5-6 mm, pain is typically non-obstructive and unresponsive to endoscopic drainage. Early referral for surgery is recommended in refractory cases, particularly in young patients with preserved function or opioid dependence. Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TPIAT) is the preferred option, especially in idiopathic or genetic disease, with the best outcomes when performed before central sensitization. Drainage procedures are ineffective, and resection has a limited role unless head-dominant disease is present [ , ]. Early Surgery Versus Endotherapy for Pain Control Randomized evidence strongly favors early surgery over an endoscopy-first approach for sustained pain control in painful obstructive CP. In the ESCAPE trial, early surgery produced a significantly lower mean Izbicki pain score over 18 months than step-up endotherapy (37 vs 49; p=0.02), with patients undergoing fewer interventions (median one vs three procedures; p<0.001) [ ]. At long-term follow-up (~eight years), complete pain relief was achieved in 45% of patients assigned to early surgery, compared with 20% in the endoscopy-first group (p=0.01), with persistently lower pain scores (33 vs 51; p=0.003) and higher patient satisfaction. Importantly, patients who crossed over from failed endotherapy to delayed surgery had significantly worse pain outcomes than those treated surgically upfront. These data support early surgical intervention, particularly in patients with a dilated MPD, complex ductal disease, or escalating opioid requirements, while endotherapy should be reserved for carefully selected, uncomplicated cases [ ]. Management of Recurrent Pain After Surgery Recurrent pain after surgery for CP is multifactorial, arising from persistent or recurrent structural disease (such as inadequate ductal decompression, anastomotic strictures, residual stones, inflammatory head mass, pseudocysts, or disconnected duct syndrome) as well as from neuropathic and nociplastic mechanisms related to neural inflammation and central sensitization [ , ]. Management requires a structured, stepwise, multidisciplinary approach, beginning with reassessment using cross-sectional imaging and/or EUS to identify potentially correctable pathology. Endoscopic therapy is preferred as first-line reintervention when treatable ductal abnormalities are present, and revisional surgery can effectively relieve symptoms in selected patients with persistent obstructive disease or failure of endotherapy. Optimized conservative management, including PERT, strict abstinence from alcohol and smoking, neuropathic pain modulators, nutritional support, and psychosocial interventions, remains essential in all patients irrespective of prior surgical intervention [ - ]. Limitations Despite substantial advances in understanding the mechanisms and management of pain in CP, several important limitations persist. Much of the available evidence is derived from heterogeneous observational studies, small randomized trials, or expert consensus, resulting in

Endoscopic therapy is preferred as first-line reintervention when treatable ductal abnormalities are present, and revisional surgery can effectively relieve symptoms in selected patients with persistent obstructive disease or failure of endotherapy. Optimized conservative management, including PERT, strict abstinence from alcohol and smoking, neuropathic pain modulators, nutritional support, and psychosocial interventions, remains essential in all patients irrespective of prior surgical intervention [ - ]. Limitations Despite substantial advances in understanding the mechanisms and management of pain in CP, several important limitations persist. Much of the available evidence is derived from heterogeneous observational studies, small randomized trials, or expert consensus, resulting in variability in definitions of pain phenotypes, treatment endpoints, and outcome measures. Pain in CP is inherently subjective and multidimensional, yet standardized tools integrating nociceptive, neuropathic, and centrally sensitized pain components are not routinely applied in clinical practice, limiting comparability across studies. Additionally, most interventional trials focus on short- to medium-term pain relief, with limited long-term follow-up assessing the durability of the benefit, progression of pancreatic insufficiency, or opioid dependence. The relative lack of high-quality comparative trials evaluating endoscopic versus surgical strategies across clearly defined ductal and pain phenotypes further constrains evidence-based decision-making. In addition, many of the cited studies and guidelines originate from high-resource regions with specialized expertise, and the marked regional variability in access to advanced endoscopic, surgical, and multidisciplinary pain interventions further limits the generalizability of these recommendations to low-resource settings. Future directions In the management of pain in CP, there is an increasingly evident shift from a uniform, stepwise analgesic strategy toward a personalized, mechanism-based approach. Contemporary evidence underscores the heterogeneity of pain pathways in CP, encompassing ductal hypertension, ongoing inflammation, neuropathic pain, and central sensitization, which explains the frequent discordance between structural disease severity and pain outcomes. Advances in pain phenotyping, through clinical pain patterns, patient-reported outcomes, and quantitative sensory testing, offer a means to better identify centrally mediated pain states and optimize patient selection for endoscopic, surgical, or neuromodulatory therapies. Parallel progress in translational pain research and neuroimaging has enhanced understanding of peripheral and central nociceptive processing, creating opportunities for targeted pharmacologic interventions and opioid-sparing strategies. Emerging evidence underscores the value of multidisciplinary care models that integrate psychological and behavioral therapies to address the biopsychosocial nature of chronic pain. Accordingly, current guidelines and reviews call for well-designed randomized trials to validate personalized treatment algorithms, identify pain-related biomarkers, and define the optimal timing of invasive interventions, with the ultimate aim of achieving durable pain relief, improving QoL, and minimizing treatment-related morbidity in CP. Conclusions Pain in CP represents a complex clinical challenge driven by overlapping nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms that are frequently discordant with structural disease severity. Contemporary evidence supports a stepwise, mechanism-based, and multidisciplinary approach to pain management, aligning therapeutic strategies with pancreatic ductal morphology and dominant pain pathways. Conservative medical therapy remains foundational, while endoscopic, EUS-guided, and surgical interventions should be selectively employed based on clear anatomic targets and the likelihood of durable benefit. Early identification of patients unlikely to respond to repeated endotherapy and timely referral for definitive surgical management are critical to preventing central sensitization and long-term opioid dependence. Future advances in pain phenotyping, biomarkers, and personalized treatment algorithms are expected to further improve long-term pain control and QoL in patients with CP.

documents.title: AGA Institute Guideline Diagnosis and Management of Asymptomatic Pancreatic Cysts

chunks.content: Introduction Pancreatic cystic neoplasms are increasingly identified incidentally due to improved quality and increased utilization of cross-sectional imaging. – Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) account for the majority of incidentally found pancreatic cysts. , There are three general subtypes: main-duct (MD-IPMN), branch-duct (BD-IPMN), and mixed-type (MT-IPMN) which all carry varying degrees of malignant potential. The malignant risk of IPMN involving the main pancreatic duct ranges from 40 to 80% for both MD-IPMN and MT-IPMN, while the malignancy risk for BD-IPMN is more variable but considered to be much lower. – For example, for patients with BD-IPMN without worrisome features or high-risk stigmata the risk of malignancy or progression to malignancy is typically estimated at 2-3%. Given the high risk of malignancy in MD-IPMN and MT-IPMN, the recommendation is surgical resection in surgically fit patients. However, given the nuances of presentation and overall, significantly lower risk of malignancy or malignant degeneration, the management of BD-IPMN is typically non-operative surveillance and remains a topic of debate. There are several existing guidelines that aid in the decision-making process for patients, gastroenterologists, and surgeons. , – These guidelines assess several radiographic cyst characteristics associated with malignant degeneration. Cumulatively, the aim of these guidelines is assessment of risk factors associated with BD-IPMN such as cyst size, presence of a solid component or mural nodule, rate of cyst growth, cyst effect on the main pancreatic duct, and serum CA 19-9, to help in decision-making regarding resection versus non-operative surveillance strategies (typically magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or endoscopic ultrasound. The surveillance of low-risk BD-IPMN continues to be controversial, particularly in younger patients, as their natural history remains poorly understood. While the malignant transformation rate of BD-IPMN is low, the cumulative incidence of transformation increases year-by-year with an estimated 1 to 3% by 5 years, which warrants surveillance. , – While two commonly used guidelines recommend lifetime surveillance of all IPMN, recently the 2023 International Association of Pancreatology (International Consensus Guidelines) joined the 2015 American Gastroenterological Association guidelines in recommending consideration for discontinuing surveillance for stable, low-risk cysts less than 3cm in size. – Lifetime surveillance is generally recommended by the 2018 American College of Gastroenterology and the European Study Group on Cystic Tumors of the Pancreas as patients with IPMN have a “field defect” and have a 3- to 5-fold higher risk of development of de novo pancreatic cancer than the age-matched population. , , The optimal interval and duration for surveillance remain debated, and the recommendations for lifetime surveillance pose a significant burden to both patients and the healthcare system. This review examines the differences in existing guidelines, the evidence for optimal surveillance interval and duration, consideration of endpoints in surveillance, and the cost-effectiveness of nonoperative management of BD-IPMN. Comparison of Existing Guidelines There are four main guidelines, all of which combined the best available evidence and expert opinion, including the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines of the International Association of Pancreatology (International Consensus Guidelines), 2018 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG), 2018 European Study Group on Cystic Tumors of the Pancreas (European Guidelines), and the 2015 American Gastroenterological Association (AGA). Each guideline agrees that management, surgical or surveillance, should be based on characteristics of the cyst associated with malignant potential and that surveillance for lower risk BD-IPMN is necessary. However, surveillance recommendations including duration and interval vary between guidelines ( ). The International Consensus Guidelines originated in 2006 and were known as the “Sendai Criteria” as the first consensus conference was held in Sendai, Japan. These guidelines were then revised in 2012 and 2017, known as the Fukoka and revised Fukoka Guidelines , respectively, and were most recently updated and published in 2023 as the Kyoto guidelines. Pancreatic surgeons predominantly rely on these guidelines when counseling patients regarding their individualized risk and decision making. Features associated with increased risk of high-grade dysplasia (HGD) or invasive cancer are defined as high-risk stigmata (HRS) and include obstructive jaundice, enhancing mural nodule ≥5mm or solid component, main pancreatic duct dilation ≥10mm, and suspicious or positive cytology if performed. Worrisome features (WF) are defined as clinical presentation with acute pancreatitis, increased serum CA19-9, new onset or acute exacerbation of diabetes within the past year, overall cyst size ≥3cm, enhancing mural nodule 5-9mm, abrupt change in caliber of pancreatic duct with distal pancreatic atrophy, lymphadenopathy, and growth rate of ≥2.5mm per year. Patients without HRS or WFs are recommended to undergo short interval follow-up based on cyst size, and, in the case of multifocal cysts, the surveillance should be based on the size of the largest cyst. The 2023 International Consensus Guidelines recommend surveillance intervals based on cyst size. For cysts <2cm, the recommendation is follow-up with MRI in 6 months once then every 18 months if stable. For cysts 2-3cm, MRI should be done every 6 months for one year then

5-9mm, abrupt change in caliber of pancreatic duct with distal pancreatic atrophy, lymphadenopathy, and growth rate of ≥2.5mm per year. Patients without HRS or WFs are recommended to undergo short interval follow-up based on cyst size, and, in the case of multifocal cysts, the surveillance should be based on the size of the largest cyst. The 2023 International Consensus Guidelines recommend surveillance intervals based on cyst size. For cysts <2cm, the recommendation is follow-up with MRI in 6 months once then every 18 months if stable. For cysts 2-3cm, MRI should be done every 6 months for one year then every 12 months if stable. For cysts ≥3cm, MRI should be done every 6 months. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) can be considered when changes in MRI are noted. Revised from the 2017 International Consensus Guidelines, the updated 2023 guidelines now consider stopping surveillance for patients with BD-IPMN <2cm without WF/HRS that remain unchanged for a period of 5 years. , Recommendations to discontinue surveillance are controversial and are predicated on regional health-related costs, risk of de novo ductal adenocarcinoma, and patients’ age, condition, life expectancy, etc. Additionally, surveillance should be discontinued in patients who are unfit for surgery or have a life-expectancy of <10 years. The remaining guidelines are predominantly used by gastroenterologists in assessing BD-IPMN associated patient risk. The 2018 European Guidelines group the risk factors predictive of HGD or invasive cancer into “absolute indications” and “relative indications” for surgery. The absolute indications mirror the HRS in the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines, and the relative indications are similar to that of WF with the exception of growth rate (≥5mm/year compared to ≥2.5mm/year in 2023 International Consensus Guideline) and cyst size (≥4cm compared to ≥3cm in all other guidelines). – Different from the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines, the 2018 European Guidelines on surveillance are not based on cyst size but instead recommend a 6-month follow-up in the first year and annually thereafter with MRI or EUS and CA19-9 for all cysts. The European Guidelines recommend MRI as the preferred imaging modality, with EUS reserved for selected cases. Although the cyst size does not change the interval or duration of surveillance, the European Guidelines do recommend consideration of surgical resection once a cyst size ≥4cm. The 2018 ACG Guideline bases surveillance on cyst size. The ACG stratifies cysts into four groups: <1cm, 1-1.9cm, 2-2.9cm, and ≥3cm. For cysts <1cm in size, MRI is recommended every 2 years for 4 years with consideration for lengthening the interval thereafter if no changes. For those 1-2cm, MRI is recommended annually for 3 years then every 2 years for 4 years with consideration for lengthening the interval thereafter if no changes. BD-IPMN 2-3cm should undergo MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years then MRI annually for 4 years then increase the interval thereafter if no changes. Those >3cm should be discussed by a multidisciplinary group and alternate MRI and EUS every 6 months for 3 years then annually for 4 years. The AGA Guidelines were established in 2015 and address only patients with asymptomatic cysts. Similar to the 2018 European Guidelines, the recommended surveillance is not based on cyst size. The AGA recommends that cysts <3cm without a solid component or main pancreatic duct dilation should undergo surveillance. The AGA is the only guideline stating that two of these features must be present to undergo either EUS or resection. The recommended surveillance strategy is MRI in 1 year then every 2 years for a total of 5 years. If there has been no change in cyst size or characteristics in 5 years, the AGA recommends discontinuing surveillance. The 2015 AGA Guidelines err on specificity with the goal of only resecting patients with HGD or invasive cancer, while remaining guidelines have higher sensitivity with the goal of not missing patients with potential malignant degeneration or in situ malignancy ( ). There have been several studies investigating the sensitivity and specificity of the 2017 International Consensus, 2018 European, 2018 ACG, and 2015 AGA Guidelines ( ). – As previously stated, the low sensitivity of the 2015 AGA guideline indicates higher rates of missing cysts with HGD or invasive cancer, however, the high specificity indicates that unnecessary surgery is recommended less often. Conversely, high sensitivity of remaining guidelines with lower specificity contributes to greater likelihood of not missing HGD or invasive cancer at the expense of performing more resections. As the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines were recently published, there has not been adequate time to study their performance, however, it is assumed that they would perform similarly to 2017 International Consensus Guidelines. Conversely, high sensitivity of remaining guidelines with lower specificity contributes to greater likelihood of not missing HGD or invasive cancer at the expense of performing more resections. As the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines were recently published, there has not been adequate time to study their performance, however, it is assumed that they would perform similarly to 2017 International Consensus Guidelines. Interval and Duration of Surveillance Although the need for surveillance is agreed upon by all guidelines, the optimal interval and duration is still debated. As we have discussed, the 2023 International Consensus and the AGA Guidelines are the only two guidelines that recommend considering discontinuing surveillance after a five-year period in the setting of cyst stability. , Although low, there is a persistent risk that indolent BD-IPMN could experience malignant transformation, especially if they experience changes within the first 5 years, with the cumulative incidence increasing yearly and estimated to be 0.94-3.3% by 5 years, 2.3-6.6% by 10 years, and 7.6-15% by 15 years. , , In addition, the field defect that leads to IPMN formation increases the overall likelihood of de novo carcinoma in patients and hence the enthusiasm for surveillance in fit patients. The goal of surveillance should be to detect cysts at risk of developing invasive cancer before becoming invasive, increasing overall survival and decreasing disease-specific mortality. Thus, factors to consider when determining the interval and duration of surveillance, particularly of low-risk BD IPMN, include cyst characteristics both at the time of diagnosis and changes over time, patient age, life expectancy, and comorbid conditions. Cyst Characteristics: At the Time of Diagnosis and Changes Over Time Mural Nodule and Solid Component Two features consistently recognized as either high-risk features or indications for surgical resection by all guidelines, surgeons, and gastroenterologists are the presence of a contrast-enhanced mural nodule or solid component. – Although mural nodules and solid components are different (mural nodule is solid tissue arising from the wall of the cyst and projecting into the cyst cavity whereas a solid component is solid tissue neighboring the cyst wall), the guidelines often use them interchangeably and they are both harbingers of malignancy. One meta-analysis with 816 patients who underwent surgery found solid component to be a strong predictor of underlying malignancy with an odds ratio (OR) of 7.73 (95% CI: 3.38-17.67). Another meta-analysis including 1452 patients found the presence of a mural nodule to have an OR of 9.3 (95% CI: 5.3-16.1) for malignant degneretaion. The 2023 International Consensus and 2018 European Guidelines recommend resection of BD-IPMN with mural nodules, however, the optimal size cutoff of mural nodules has not been defined. , – A retrospective analysis of 188 surgically treated patients found that enhancing mural nodules ≥5mm was an independent predictor of malignancy. Another retrospective study of 329 patients who underwent resection for IPMN found that the frequency of HGD was significantly higher in patients who underwent surgery with a mural nodule ≥5mm compared with those <5mm or without a mural nodule. Mural nodule size >9mm was found to be independently associated with invasive IPMN and had an accuracy of 94.5% in predicting HGD or invasive cancer. A predictive model reported a cutoff ≥10mm is more sensitive at predicting HGD or invasive cancer than a mural nodule between 5 and 10mm. It is evident that mural nodule portends a risk of malignancy and BD-IPMN with nodules, irrespective of size, should be selected for resection in fit patients. Mural nodularity/solid component should be distinguished from a mucin ball. The difference is most readily detected by a gastroenterologist with expertise in EUS. A mucin ball is typically formed by solidified mucin, is at times seen during evaluation typically as a non-enhancing mural nodule, and importantly does not have increased risk of malignant transformation. , Molecular Analyses Molecular analysis of cyst fluid or sampling of nodular component might help prognosticate risk associated with the operation versus risks of surveillance in a patient with high-risk stigmata. , The 2023 International Consensus Guidelines are the first to mention molecular analysis of cyst fluid obtained via EUS, recognizing that certain mutations may be useful in identifying high-risk cysts. Mutations in KRAS and/or GNAS have been shown to have high sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of IPMN, while mutations in TP5, SMAD4, CDKN2A, PTEN, and PIK3CA have been associated with HGD and invasive caner. – Next-generation sequencing shows promise in identifying mutations associated with HGD and invasive disease, enabling earlier and more accurate prognostication and risk-stratification in a patient’s clinical course. IPMN Size The role of cyst size in determining risk of progression is controversial given the relatively unknown natural history of BD-IPMN. Currently, only the 2023 International Consensus and 2018 ACG Guidelines recommend surveillance intervals based on size. , Variation also exists in cyst size

to have high sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of IPMN, while mutations in TP5, SMAD4, CDKN2A, PTEN, and PIK3CA have been associated with HGD and invasive caner. – Next-generation sequencing shows promise in identifying mutations associated with HGD and invasive disease, enabling earlier and more accurate prognostication and risk-stratification in a patient’s clinical course. IPMN Size The role of cyst size in determining risk of progression is controversial given the relatively unknown natural history of BD-IPMN. Currently, only the 2023 International Consensus and 2018 ACG Guidelines recommend surveillance intervals based on size. , Variation also exists in cyst size cutoff for consideration of EUS or surgical intervention; most guidelines recommend consideration of EUS or surgical intervention at a cyst size of ≥3cm, whereas 2018 European Guidelines use a size of ≥4cm. In a meta-analysis of 16 studies including 1058 patients, size ≥3cm was the strongest predictive factor for underlying malignancy with an OR of 62.4 (95% CI: 30.8-126.3). Although this meta-analysis identified a large OR, the confidence interval is very broad and it is likely that size was a harbinger of more aggressive BD-IPMN features. Another systematic review including 644 patients reported an OR of 2.97 (95% CI: 1.82-4.85) for cysts ≥3cm to have underlying HGD or invasive cancer. In this study, 43% of patients with a cyst ≥3cm had HGD or invasive cancer compared to 22% of patients with a cyst size <3cm, suggesting a threshold of ≥3cm for more intense surveillance or surgery may be appropriate, but also showing that cyst size is not the only important feature, as malignancy can be seen in BD-IPMN <3cm. Some studies have demonstrated increasing incidence of malignant transformation with larger initial cyst size, lending evidence towards size-based intervals. , – A recent international, multicenter retrospective study found that the prevalence of WF/HRS and malignant conversion varied based on initial cyst size with cysts ≥2cm having a shorter time to progression and those ≥3cm had a 28.5% rate of malignant degeneration. Since the overwhelming majority of BD-IPMNs are discovered incidentally, it remains unclear if these findings represent lead-time bias, meaning that the larger cysts may have been present for longer but may have progressed at a similar rate if they were all identified at the same size. Alternatively, it may indicate that once a cyst reaches a certain size, it is an indication that it is much more likely to have malignant transformation. For example, a retrospective analysis evaluated morphologic changes in 1369 patients based on initial cyst size and found that cysts >2cm at the time of diagnosis had significantly higher growth rate, likelihood of MPD dilation, cyst wall thickening, development of WF, and annual malignant conversion rate. Regardless, BD-IPMN of greater size with solid component deserve greater consideration for closer surveillance, EUS, or resection based on cyst characteristics. Furthermore, determining duration of surveillance has been debated. Initially, only the 2015 AGA Guidelines recommended stopping surveillance in low-risk cysts; however, the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines have now adopted considering discontinuing surveillance for cysts <2cm that remain stable without WF/HRS over a 5-year period. BD-IPMN are known to have a relatively slow progression time, and despite the low incidence of progression, studies have found the risk to be persistent beyond 5 years and may even increase with one study showing an incidence as high as 12%. , , , – In contrast, a multicenter retrospective study of 982 patients found the incidence of pancreatic cancer to be <1% in patients without significant changes in the first 5 years. Another multicenter retrospective study evaluating 3844 patients demonstrated that the risk of malignancy is not significantly higher than the age-matched general population in patients with stable cysts for 5 years who are either age ≥75 with a cyst <3cm or age ≥65 with a cyst ≤1.5cm. Rate of Growth All guidelines aside from the 2015 AGA Guidelines provide recommendations for either proceeding to EUS or surgery based on rate of cyst growth, however, the data on the threshold rate of growth for predicting progression to HGD or invasive cancer is limited. , , , – A recent systematic review found the rate of growth as a predictor of HGD or invasive cancer to be 0.96mm/year to 3.5mm/year. A retrospective study of 1036 patients found cyst growth rate of ≥2.5mm/year to be a significant predictor of development of invasive cancer. This cutoff of 2.5mm/year remains a WF in the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines. A smaller retrospective study including only 50 patients found that a growth rate of 3.5mm/year predicted malignancy with a sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 91%. Some studies have demonstrated an association between rapid growth in cysts and increasing WF, suggesting that follow up intervals should be based in part on growth rate. , For example, a retrospective study including 189

be 0.96mm/year to 3.5mm/year. A retrospective study of 1036 patients found cyst growth rate of ≥2.5mm/year to be a significant predictor of development of invasive cancer. This cutoff of 2.5mm/year remains a WF in the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines. A smaller retrospective study including only 50 patients found that a growth rate of 3.5mm/year predicted malignancy with a sensitivity of 88% and specificity of 91%. Some studies have demonstrated an association between rapid growth in cysts and increasing WF, suggesting that follow up intervals should be based in part on growth rate. , For example, a retrospective study including 189 patients found that cysts that developed WF had a significantly higher growth rate of 2.84mm/year compared to 0.23mm/year in those that remained low-risk, however no patients in this study developed HRS, HGD, or invasive cancer. These studies suggest initial short-term follow up to determine cysts with rapid growth that may require more intense surveillance. Development of Worrisome Features/High-Risk Stigmata There are multiple features considered to be worrisome or high-risk by each guideline due to their association with increased risk for HGD or invasive cancer ( ). The development of multiple WFs has been shown to significantly increase the risk of HGD and invasive cancer. , , , – An analysis of 810 patients from two tertiary referral centers found an incremental increase in accuracy of diagnosis of HGD/invasive cancer with each additional WF, reaching 100% with 4 WFs. Similarly, a multicenter retrospective study including 292 patients found that the development of an additional WF or HRS was associated with a significantly higher rate of HGD. Another study identified that ≥2 WFs was associated with an increased risk of HGD/malignancy compared to 1 WF. The likelihood of HGD/invasive cancer has been shown to be lower in the presence of only WFs as opposed to HRS. , , , For example, the previously discussed retrospective study of 810 patients found that the risk of HGD/invasive carcinoma with 3 WFs was comparable to that of having a single HRS. Additionally, another study showed progression of a low-risk cyst (without WF/HRS at baseline) to HRS, but not WF, was associated with significantly higher risk of invasive cancer. In a retrospective study 1101 patients from the Mayo Clinic, patients with HRS had a 5-year risk of malignancy of 49.7% compared to 5.1% with WFs only. While each WF/HRS carries its own risk of HGD/invasive cancer, the relative risk of each has not been completely studied and is largely unknown. Some analyses have not identified any individual WF/HRS to be a significant predictor of HGD/invasive cancer, , while others postulate that obstructive jaundice, main duct dilation (≥1 cm), and enhancing mural nodularity are predictive of malignant transformation. Multifocality The incidence of multifocal BD-IPMN, defined as two or more cysts located in different areas of the pancreas, has been reported to be 20% to 40%. , Molecular assessments have demonstrated the cysts arise independently of each other, supporting the “field defect” theory. Despite the presence of multiple cysts, several studies have shown no significant difference in survival or grade of dysplasia. , , , Conversely, one retrospective study evaluating 141 patients found a high incidence of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) concomitant with IPMN in multifocal cysts with an OR 4.11 (95% CI: 1.22-18.8). The 2023 International Consensus Guidelines recommends that management of multifocal BD-IPMN should mirror that of unifocal BD-IPMN, and that surveillance or decision to proceed to surgery should focus on the cyst with the highest risk. Patient Age and Life Expectancy The mean age of diagnosis of BD-IPMN is mid-sixties with an increase in prevalence with increasing age. , The aim of surveillance is early detection of a cyst that has undergone malignant transformation, preferably before it has become invasive cancer, allowing for early surgical intervention. However, recent studies suggest that beyond certain ages, competing risks of mortality become more significant, and the incidence of pancreatic cancer is not significantly higher than that of the age-matched general population. , , , , , Many studies evaluating age have used a combination of age with other factors such as cyst size or comorbidities. For example, a recent multicenter retrospective study found that age ≥75 (HR: 4.15, 95% CI: 1.76-9.76) and Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) (HR: 3.61, 95% CI: 1.42-9.14) were independent predictors of causes of death unrelated to IPMN or pancreatic malignancy. This study also found that in all age/CCI groupings, the risk of malignant transformation at 5 years was lower than the risk of overall mortality and was most profound in those aged ≥75 with a CCI >3. Furthermore, another study found that the risk of pancreatic cancer in patients aged 65-years or older with “trivial” BD-IPMN, defined as cysts without WFs or HRS that have remained stable for a 5-year period, is similar to

This study also found that in all age/CCI groupings, the risk of malignant transformation at 5 years was lower than the risk of overall mortality and was most profound in those aged ≥75 with a CCI >3. Furthermore, another study found that the risk of pancreatic cancer in patients aged 65-years or older with “trivial” BD-IPMN, defined as cysts without WFs or HRS that have remained stable for a 5-year period, is similar to that of the general population. A subsequent study evaluated cyst size and age, finding that the incidence of pancreatic cancer in patients aged ≥75 years with stable cysts ≤3cm without WFs or HRS for at least 5 years was not significantly higher than the general population. Additionally, patients ≥65 years of age with stable cysts sized ≤1.5cm without WFs or HRS after 5 years of surveillance did not have an increased risk of pancreatic cancer compared with the general population. In contrast to these studies, a retrospective study in Japan found a 10-fold increase in risk of pancreatic malignancy compared to the age-matched population suggesting that continued surveillance may be necessary in patients fit for surgery. A recent international, multicenter study including 3656 patients demonstrated no malignant conversion in stable cysts >3cm without WF or HRS after 5 years, and the time to progression was >10 years suggesting that surveillance can be discontinued in patients with cysts of this nature and a life expectancy ≤10 years. The 2023 International Consensus Guidelines are the first guideline to provide a recommendation on surveillance based on life expectancy, recommending considering discontinuing surveillance in patients with a life expectancy <10 years. Based on life tables published in 2023, the average life expectancy in the United States at age 65 was 18.4 years and decreased to 11.6 years at age 75. The average life expectancy at age 75 is similar to that of the life expectancy cutoff for surveillance as recommended by the 2023 International Consensus Guidelines, suggesting that the age threshold of ≥75 years proposed by some studies may be a promising threshold, though this needs to be individualized based on the overall fitness and health of the patient. While more work is needed to discern an optimal age threshold for discontinuing surveillance, these studies highlight the importance of considering competing risks of mortality and survival benefits when appraising duration of surveillance. Consideration of Comorbidities Patients diagnosed with BD-IPMN often have multiple comorbid conditions, which is expected given an aging population is associated with increased comorbidities. The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) is a widely used and validated tool to quantify comorbidity burden and comorbidity-associated mortality. Several studies have evaluated comorbidities and association with outcomes in patients with BD-IPMN by using the CCI or age-adjusted CCI. , , , , , A single-center study investigated 440 patients with low-risk cysts and found patients with an age-adjusted CCI ≥4 had a significantly higher overall mortality than those with age-adjusted CCI <4. A group from Massachusetts General Hospital described that an age-adjusted CCI of ≥7 was associated with an eightfold higher mortality unrelated to IPMN. Another group investigated cause-specific mortality in four groups (low-risk patient and cyst, low-risk patient with high-risk cyst, high-risk patient and cyst, or high-risk patient with low-risk cyst) with high-risk patients having a CCI ≥3 and high-risk cysts having main pancreatic duct dilation or cyst size ≥3cm. In all groups, the risk of non-pancreatic cancer mortality was higher than the risk of pancreatic cancer mortality. As previously discussed, CCI >3 was one of two independent predictors of causes of death unrelated to IPMN or pancreatic malignancy. When divided into groups based on age and CCI, all groups had a higher risk of overall mortality at 5 years post-diagnosis than risk of malignant progression. This was particularly true for those ≥75 years with CCI >3 who had a higher 5-year incidence of IPMN-relevant changes, but a rate of pancreatic malignancy <5% and overall mortality of >20%, indicating that factors other than pancreatic malignancy are contributing more to mortality. Decisions about surveillance for patients with limited overall survival as indicated by CCI or age-adjusted CCI should be weighed against the survival benefit surveillance provides. Some studies have found that the mortality risk from malignant transformation after 5 years in low-risk cysts is comparable to that of the mortality risk following pancreatic resection at high volume centers , , , suggesting that surveillance may not be beneficial in this population. These studies indicate that competing mortality risks should play a role in clinical decision-making and patient discussions about whether to continue surveillance as well as whether invasive or noninvasive modalities should be used in selected populations.

Some studies have found that the mortality risk from malignant transformation after 5 years in low-risk cysts is comparable to that of the mortality risk following pancreatic resection at high volume centers , , , suggesting that surveillance may not be beneficial in this population. These studies indicate that competing mortality risks should play a role in clinical decision-making and patient discussions about whether to continue surveillance as well as whether invasive or noninvasive modalities should be used in selected populations. Patient Desire/Willingness Before initiating a surveillance program, it is important to have a thorough discussion with the patient, considering their preferences along with the previously discussed factors. Since the goal of surveillance is to detect and then surgically intervene on cysts prior to transformation into an invasive cancer, the conversations should include discussions about surgery and the associated morbidity and mortality. Morbidity and mortality after distal pancreatectomy are thought to be lower than after pancreatoduodenectomy. Although there have been improvements in mortality, major morbidity with pancreas surgery is still estimated to be 30-46% for pancreaticoduodenectomy and 9-24% for distal pancreatectomy. , , – The mortality from IPMN-related causes has been shown to be similar to that of mortality related to pancreatic surgery at a high volume facility, both around 2%. Current mortality statistics for surgical resection are likely under-reporting true mortality of resections with 90-day mortality after pancreatoduodenectomy approaching 6.5-9%. – The diagnosis and surveillance of IPMN may also impose a psychological burden on patients. Some studies have examined the emotional and psychological impact IPMN surveillance and surgery have on patients, revealing varied outcomes. One study found that patients’ baseline mental and physical quality of life were not different from that of the general population and remained comparable during surveillance over a two-year period. Similarly, another study evaluating 232 patients undergoing surveillance found no negative impact of health-related quality of life or anxiety levels. In contrast, one study comparing patients in surveillance to those who underwent surgery found that patients under surveillance felt less healthy and had higher levels of stress and anxiety than those who had surgery. Considering the risks of malignant transformation, surgical risks, and the emotional and psychological impact should guide discussions with patients. If a patient is unwilling to undergo surgery, continued surveillance may either alleviate anxiety or be futile. Cost-Effectiveness The increasing incidence of BD-IPMN poses a clinical challenge and carries societal and personal economic consequences as well. There have been several studies modeling the cost-effectiveness of management strategies in IPMN, most of which compare surgery, guideline-based surveillance, and do-nothing approaches using some combination of quality-adjusted life years (QALY), cost, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) as the primary outcomes. – A 2010 analysis out of Massachusetts General Hospital compared surgery, surveillance, and no surveillance approaches among 60-year-old patients and demonstrated that surgery is the most effective strategy, but it is also the most expensive. Surveillance can be a cost-effective strategy depending on the age of the cohort with continued cost-effectiveness until the age of 78, suggesting that above this age, surveillance is no longer cost-effective and stopping surveillance can be considered. Another study modeled cost-effectiveness in a population with 65-year-old patients and found surgery to be the least expensive but also the least effective strategy in terms of QALY gained, while surveillance was the most cost-effective if the patient is surgically fit. A 2020 model of 60-year-old patients found that surveillance based on consensus guidelines is the least cost-effective strategy when compared to surgery and a do-nothing approach. However, with improved specificity, meaning avoiding unnecessary resection in those without HGD or invasive cancer, surveillance becomes more cost-effective and improves survival. Another group used Monte Carlo modeling to compare clinical outcomes and economic factors between the 2017 International Consensus Guidelines and 2015 AGA guidelines in a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 people. The model found that the 2015 AGA guidelines had more missed cancers but cost significantly less and had fewer surgery-related mortalities. The more intensive strategy based on the 2017 International Consensus Guidelines spent $8000 more per patient, costing an additional $3.6 million per additional cancer detected, and had higher surgery-related mortality but fewer missed cancers. The true dollar amounts are difficult to ascertain due to opaqueness in the reimbursement schema existing in healthcare systems. The current guidelines have high sensitivities, aside from the AGA , – , , allowing them to detect HGD or invasive cancer. The true dollar amounts are difficult to ascertain due to opaqueness in the reimbursement schema existing in healthcare systems. The current guidelines have high sensitivities, aside from the AGA , – , , allowing them to detect HGD or invasive cancer. The specificities, on the other hand, are quite low varying with guideline used. , – , Given that the majority of BD-IPMN undergo surveillance, it is reasonable to focus on creating more specific tools and guidelines to detect malignant cysts and morphologic changes to avoid subjecting patients to unnecessary operations, undue financial and psychological burdens, and to improve the cost-effectiveness of surveillance. A recent model out of Japan compared the cost-effectiveness of continued versus discontinued surveillance and found that not only did age impact cost-effectiveness, so did sex, and comorbidities. The age at which surveillance was no longer cost-effective in men was 76 to 78, while the age varied for females depending on the size of the cyst with the lowest cutoff being 70 years for cysts <2cm and the highest being 81 years for cysts 3cm or more. Another model evaluated upfront resection for BD-IPMN with WFs and found it to be more effective in terms of cancer-free and overall survival than aggressive surveillance in patients with a life expectancy of at least 18 years. In practicality, selecting elderly patients for pancreatic surgery is challenging. Patients who are elderly, in their eighth or ninth decade of life are unlikely to benefit from surgery to resect BD-IPMN as the risk of malignant degeneration is very low. For patients with MD-IPMN or MT-IPMN the calculations might differ based on patients’ functional status, extent of comorbid conditions, and wishes. The majority of studies have found an age above which surveillance is no longer cost-effective, suggesting that increasing age may mitigate any cost-effective benefit of surveillance. Most of these studies are limited by considering only BD-IPMN located in the head of the pancreas and/or using outdated guidelines. Nonetheless, the findings suggest that to improve the cost-effective management of BD-IPMN, more work is needed to increase the specificity of guidelines and diagnostic tools along with more information regarding the natural history of IPMN. Conclusions As the incidence of IPMN, particularly BD-IPMN, continues to rise, managing the condition becomes increasingly important yet challenging due to the increasing age of those diagnosed and the uncertainty of the natural history of BD-IPMN. Deciding on surveillance strategies – including their intensity and duration – and selecting appropriate surgical candidates requires careful consideration of multiple factors. Emerging insights, particularly in molecular analysis techniques, are expected to further refine and guide management decisions in the future.

chunks.content: Abbreviations AGA Antigliadin Antibodies AGREE‐II Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II auto‐HSCT Autologous Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation BMD Bone Mineral Density CeD Coeliac Disease CoE certainty of evidence DAE Device‐Assisted Enteroscopy DGP Deamidated Gluten Peptides DH Dermatitis Herpetiformis DXA Dual Energy Absorptiometry Measurement EATL Enteropathy‐associated T cell Lymphoma ESPGHAN European Society Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition ESsCD European Society for the Study of Coeliac Disease FODMAPs fermentable oligo di‐mono‐saccharides and polyols GFD Gluten‐Free Diet GR grade of recommendation GRADE Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation HLA Human Leucocyte Antigen IBD Inflammatory Bowel Disease IBS Irritable Bowel Syndrome ICI immune checkpoint inhibitor IEL Intraepithelial Lymphocytes IgA anti‐EMA anti‐Endomysial Antibodies LE Level of Evidence NA Not Applicable NCWS Non‐Coeliac Wheat Allergy NPV Negative Predictive Value POCT Point‐of‐care testing PPV Positive Predictive Value QoL Quality of Life RCD‐I Refractory Coeliac Disease type 1 RCD‐II Refractory Coeliac Disease type 2 SNCD Seronegative Coeliac Disease T1DM Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus TG2 Tissue Transglutaminase 2 UGPS ungraded good practice statement ULN Upper Limit of Normal VCE Video Capsule Endoscopy 1 Introduction The 2025 European Society for the Study of Coeliac Disease (ESsCD) guidelines on coeliac disease (CeD) are presented in two complementary parts. Part 1 focuses on the diagnostic approach [ ], whilst part 2‐ the present document‐addresses disease management, follow‐up, and the approach to patients with persistent or recurrent symptoms despite gluten‐free diet (GFD) and refractory CeD (RCD). Together, these updates provide an integrated framework encompassing the full spectrum of adult CeD care. These guidelines present an update to the 2019 ESsCD guidelines on the Management of CeD and Other Gluten‐Related Disorders [ ]. Since their publication, emerging evidence has prompted substantial refinements in dietary management, structured follow‐up, and the care of patients with complex or treatment‐refractory disease. Key developments include: Dietary Management: Maintenance of a lifelong strict GFD remains central to treatment, with new emphasis on nutritional adequacy, metabolic health, prevention of deficiencies and aspects of food labelling. The safety of gluten‐free oats is clarified, and a low‐FODMAP dietary approach is proposed for patients with persistent gastrointestinal symptoms despite histological remission. Follow‐Up & Monitoring: The updated guidance recognises two possible follow‐up strategies—a tailored model adapted to patient‐specific needs and risk profiles, and a standardised model with fixed assessment intervals. Both approaches prioritise multidisciplinary evaluation, including telemedicine integration and systematic assessment of adherence, psychosocial wellbeing, and quality of life (QoL). Patient Support Groups are recognized as an integral part of long‐term management. Transition from Paediatric to Adult Care: A “coeliac passport” is recommended to facilitate smooth transition and ensuring continuity of care, summarising key medical and dietary information. Management of RCD: Updated recommendations define diagnostic criteria and therapeutic strategies, including the potential use of targeted immunosuppressive therapies such as JAK inhibitors, cladribine or fludarabine, and autologous haematopoietic stem‐cell transplantation for selected patients. Newly addressed areas: Management of confirmed exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in CeD, stratified bone‐health monitoring, psychosocial support, pregnancy management, risk‐based family screening and the potential use of gluten immunogenic peptides (GIPs) as an adjunct tool for monitoring adherence to the GFD. Collectively, these guideline revisions reflect a paradigm shift towards personalised, proactive, and multidisciplinary care for adults with CeD. The overarching goals are to improve disease control, enhance QoL, and reduce the risk of long‐term complications through evidence‐based, patient‐centred management. 2 Summary of Recommendations 2.1 Methodology We followed the methodology for assessing the quality of evidence and risk of bias as described in Part 1 of these ESsCD guidelines [ ]. Whilst maintaining the same approach to grading the overall certainty of evidence according to the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology, https://www.gradeworkinggroup.org/ , we applied the following tools depending on study design: the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 2) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), ROBINS‐I for non‐randomized studies of interventions, QUADAS‐2 for diagnostic accuracy studies, AMSTAR‐2 for systematic reviews, and the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for observational cohort and cross‐sectional studies. 3 Questions, Recommendations and Evidence: Management of Adults With Coeliac Disease The management of CeD aims to relieve symptoms, promote mucosal healing, restore nutritional status, prevent complications, and optimize quality of life. The cornerstone of treatment is a strict, lifelong GFD, supported by expert dietetic input and ongoing adherence monitoring, whilst emerging dietary approaches, such as low‐FODMAP strategies, may be considered in selected cases. Comprehensive care also includes screening for comorbidities, supporting psychosocial well‐being, monitoring bone mineral density, providing vaccinations when indicated, and addressing associated conditions, including autoimmune disorders, metabolic syndrome, and extra‐intestinal manifestations. Tailored strategies are required for special populations, evolving clinical scenarios such as CeD–like enteropathy during treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors, and patients with co‐existing conditions.
